Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

our board-game lending shelf is in the east room of the Marlow Community Hall, between the noticeboard and the low radiator. The hall committee agreed that the shelf could stay there, and the group now looks after it. There are two wide shelves, a small basket for cards and dice, and a clipboard on a hook at the side. The window above the shelf gets afternoon light, though the room is usually dim when the evening meetings begin. We put a paper label on each box with its shelf number, and a matching number is written in the lending book.

The collection has grown to 46 games, not all of which are suitable for the same occasion. There are short games that take about fifteen minutes, longer strategy games, family games, and a few games that are more enjoyable with a larger group. The red sticker means a game is generally playable in under half an hour, while the blue sticker means that it is usually best with at least four people. These are guides rather than rules, since some groups play quickly and others take their time. We have three copies of Orchard Road because it was requested often last winter, and one copy of Lantern Market, which is newer and has only been borrowed twice so far. A couple of boxes are slightly worn around the corners, but their contents have been checked.

People can borrow a game for up to two weeks. They write their name, the game number, and the date taken out in the book, then add the return date when they bring it back. The usual arrangement is to return games on Wednesday evening, when one of the supper group members is at the hall, but borrowers can also leave them with the caretaker during opening hours. If a game is returned with a piece missing, it is placed in the basket marked “Needs checking” rather than put straight back on the shelf. That detail matters because the caretaker does not check game contents, and another borrower might otherwise take the box before anyone notices. We check the piece list in the box and note any missing item in the book before deciding whether the game can go back out.

There is a short note inside the lending book that says, “Please let us know if a box is damaged or a piece is missing.” It is there so people are not worried about bringing something back in imperfect condition. In February, a borrower returned Fox and Fable with a split cardboard insert, but all the cards and counters were present. The group taped the insert on the inside, and the game was available again the following week. We do not charge people for ordinary wear, and nobody has been asked to replace a game. Occasionally, a box comes back later than the date written down; we send a friendly reminder rather than treating it as a problem. Most people return games on time, and a few borrowers write the date in their phone as soon as they sign the book.

1. When a new game is donated, we first check that the box has a title and that the contents list is included. One person counts the pieces, while another reads the list, which takes a little longer but makes mix-ups less likely. The game then gets a number in the order it is added, a label, and a line in the book with its title and player range. If the instructions are in another language, we note that on the label so borrowers can see it before taking the game. The group does not make a new set of rules for a game, and donations are not added until the contents have been checked.

2. On Wednesday evenings, the person on shelf duty looks over the book and checks whether any game is due back. They also put returned boxes on the table for a quick look before replacing them. If the weather has been wet, we leave a box on the table until the outside is dry, because damp cardboard can soften at the edges. The shelf duty is shared among six members, and a simple rota is clipped to the inside of the cupboard door. If the person named on the rota cannot come, they usually arrange a swap in the group chat; the rota is updated only when the swap is confirmed.

3. The lending shelf is for people who use the hall, but a borrower does not need to be a member of the supper group. A small card beside the clipboard gives the borrowing steps and explains that games should not be left outside the hall entrance. The hall closes at nine, so anyone using the caretaker handover needs to return the box before that time. We have not put a deposit system in place. Perhaps that would suit a much larger collection, but at the moment the book and the Wednesday check have been enough to keep track of what is out.

The group talks about the shelf at its monthly supper, usually for only a few minutes because there are other things to arrange. In March, one person suggested setting aside a shelf for games that work well with two players, and the group agreed to try it with the next three donations. The space is not marked yet, and no games have been moved; the idea is to see whether borrowers use that category before changing the labels. Another member said, “I like knowing there’s something new to try, even when I only have an hour.” That comment came up while people were discussing the shorter games, rather than the collection as a whole. The current signs are handwritten on cream card, and one is slightly crooked because the tape keeps lifting near the radiator.

A folding table is sometimes set beside the shelf during the hall’s autumn open evening, so visitors can look through games without blocking the noticeboard. The group has not decided whether to do that this year, because the open evening date has not been confirmed. If it goes ahead, the shelf team would bring out only the games that have complete pieces and keep the lending book by the clipboard, not on the table. This is the same check used on ordinary Wednesday returns. The room is shared with a sewing circle on Thursday afternoons, and their members leave the games where they are; the shelf is not part of their equipment. The caretaker asked for a second basket last month, and the group has placed one beneath the clipboard for the cards and dice that occasionally turn up loose after a game night.

The little collection is still managed by the Wednesday group, with donations coming in at different times rather than through a formal drive. The member who records new games writes in pencil first, in case a title needs correcting, and inks the entry after the label has been checked. We usually hear about a possible donation before it arrives, though once a box was left with the caretaker without a note, and the group waited until the donor was identified before adding it. On the shelf, the games are arranged by number, not by type, because that makes the lending book quicker to use. A printed list of the titles is kept on the table near the door for people who want to browse before walking across the room.
